questions.stem: A body of mass 4 kg is acted upon by a net force of 20 N. Its acceleration is
Newton's first law of motion is also known as the
questions.explanation: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force — this defines inertia.

questions.stem: The SI unit of force is the
questions.explanation: $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg m s}^{-2}$, the SI unit of force.

questions.stem: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s$^{-1}$ in 10 s. The net force required is
questions.explanation: $a = \Delta v/\Delta t = 2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, so $F = ma = 1000 \times 2 = 2000\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: The total momentum of an isolated system of bodies is conserved in the absence of
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation holds when the net external force on the system is zero; internal forces (like collisions) don't change total momentum anyway.

questions.stem: A 2 kg body moving at 3 m s$^{-1}$ collides head-on with a 3 kg body moving at 2 m s$^{-1}$ in the opposite direction, and they stick together. Their common velocity after collision is
questions.explanation: Taking the 2 kg body's direction as positive: $p = 2(3) + 3(-2) = 0$, so $v = p/(m_1+m_2) = 0$.

questions.stem: The forward thrust on a rocket as it ejects exhaust gases is explained by
questions.explanation: As gas is expelled backward with momentum, the rocket gains equal and opposite momentum forward, by conservation of momentum.

questions.stem: The coefficient of static friction between two surfaces is generally
options: greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction
less than the coefficient of kinetic friction
equal to the coefficient of kinetic friction
unrelated to the coefficient of kinetic friction
questions.explanation: It takes more force to start relative motion than to sustain it, so $\mu_s > \mu_k$ in general.

questions.stem: A 5 kg block slides on a horizontal surface with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. Taking $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, the frictional force on it is
questions.explanation: $f = \mu mg = 0.2 \times 5 \times 10 = 10\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: For a body just about to slide down a rough inclined plane under its own weight, the angle of repose $\theta$ satisfies
questions.explanation: At the verge of sliding, $mg\sin\theta = \mu mg\cos\theta$, giving $\tan\theta = \mu$.

questions.stem: For a car of mass $m$ turning on a frictionless banked road of radius $r$ at speed $v$, the banking angle $\theta$ must satisfy
questions.explanation: Resolving the normal reaction with no friction: $N\sin\theta = mv^2/r$ and $N\cos\theta = mg$, giving $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$.

questions.stem: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force on the body is directed
options: towards the centre of the circle
away from the centre of the circle
questions.explanation: Centripetal force always points toward the centre, causing the change in direction of velocity needed for circular motion.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg stone tied to a 1 m string moves in a horizontal circle at 2 revolutions per second. The tension in the string (centripetal force) is approximately
questions.explanation: $F = m\omega^2 r$, with $\omega = 2\pi n = 4\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$: $F = 0.5 \times (4\pi)^2 \times 1 \approx 79\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: Walking forward on the ground is possible mainly because of
options: Newton's third law — the ground pushes back on the foot
the first law of motion alone
questions.explanation: The foot pushes backward on the ground; by Newton's third law, the ground pushes forward on the foot, propelling the body.

The same 60 kg person now stands in a lift accelerating downward at 2 m s$^{-2}$. Taking $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, the apparent weight is
Impulse delivered to a body equals its change in
questions.explanation: Impulse–momentum theorem: $J = \int F\,dt = \Delta p$.

questions.stem: A 0.15 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m s$^{-1}$ and rebounds elastically with the same speed. The magnitude of change in momentum is
questions.explanation: $\Delta p = m(v - (-v)) = 0.15 \times 24 = 3.6\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$.

questions.stem: In an Atwood machine, masses 2 kg and 3 kg hang from a string over a frictionless pulley. Taking $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, the acceleration of the system is
For the same Atwood machine (masses 2 kg and 3 kg, $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$), the tension in the string is
questions.explanation: $T = m_1(g+a) = 2(10+2) = 24\ \text{N}$, consistent with $T = m_2(g-a) = 3(10-2) = 24\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: A pseudo (fictitious) force is introduced when analysing motion from
options: both inertial and non-inertial frames equally
questions.explanation: Pseudo forces are needed only in accelerating (non-inertial) frames, to make Newton's second law appear to hold there.

questions.stem: Static friction is best described as a
options: self-adjusting force, up to a maximum limit
constant force independent of applied force
force that is always zero on rough surfaces
force always equal to its maximum value
questions.explanation: Static friction adjusts to exactly balance the applied force (up to $\mu_s N$) so that the body stays at rest.

questions.stem: A body moving at 10 m s$^{-1}$ on a rough horizontal surface ($\mu = 0.5$, $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$) decelerates due to friction at a rate of
questions.explanation: Deceleration $a = \mu g = 0.5 \times 10 = 5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

questions.stem: Using the previous body (initial speed 10 m s$^{-1}$, deceleration 5 m s$^{-2}$), the time it takes to stop is
questions.explanation: $v = u - at \Rightarrow 0 = 10 - 5t \Rightarrow t = 2\ \text{s}$.

questions.stem: Newton's second law of motion, expressed in terms of momentum $p$, is written as
questions.explanation: The general form of Newton's second law is $F = dp/dt$, which reduces to $F=ma$ when mass is constant.
